assignmentHtml.task: Challenge S: Compare DART deflection experiment with Lucy's Dinkinesh/Selam observations. Distinguish: (1) an intervention with measured dynamical consequences (DART) from imaging that constrains morphology and formation hypotheses (Lucy); (2) DART mutual-orbit vs heliocentric quantities separately. Explain which conclusions depend on object identity, structure, geometry, measurement time, or model choice, and which cannot be generalized to a different target. Find: Thomas et al. 2023 Nature (mutual orbit period change), Makadia et al. 2026 Science Advances (heliocentric changes), NASA DART pages, Lucy Dinkinesh papers. Note DART hit Dimorphos (not Didymos), momentum enhancement β=2.2-4.9, rubble-pile structure, warning time requirements.
assignmentHtml.context: Challenge S needs to distinguish intervention/experiment from observation/imaging. DART: kinetic impactor on ~160m rubble-pile Dimorphos (Sept 26, 2022), mutual orbit shortened by 33.0±1.0 min (Thomas 2023), refined to 33 min 15 s (Naidu 2024); heliocentric Δv = -11.7±1.3 μm/s (Makadia 2026). Generalization limits: size (~160m tested), structure (rubble-pile, 35% porosity), warning time (decades needed). Lucy: Dinkinesh is main-belt asteroid with satellite Selam (contact binary), flyby Nov 1, 2023 — imaging constrains morphology/formation but does not intervene. Contact binary structure belongs to Selam, not primary Dinkinesh.
assignmentHtml.expected_output: Detailed comparison dossier for Challenge S with: experiment vs observation matrix, per-mission quantity tables with separate mutual-orbit and heliocentric columns, generalization limits with dependencies (object identity, structure, geometry, time, models), original paper citations with URLs.

answerHtml:
COMPARISON DOSSIER: DART DEFLECTION EXPERIMENT vs. LUCY DINKINESH/SELAM OBSERVATIONS

(1) INTERVENTION vs. OBSERVATION

DART — Controlled kinetic impact experiment:
• NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft into Dimorphos on 26 Sept 2022 at 23:14 UTC, impact velocity ~6.6 km/s [NASA Didymos page]. This is an active intervention designed to measure dynamical consequences.
• Produced measurable changes in both the mutual orbit (Dimorphos around Didymos) and the heliocentric orbit (Didymos system around Sun).
• Published results: Thomas et al. 2023 Nature (mutual orbit), Cheng et al. 2023 Nature (momentum transfer), Naidu et al. 2024 Planetary Science Journal (refined orbit/shape), Makadia et al. 2026 Science Advances (heliocentric deflection).

Lucy Dinkinesh/Selam — Passive imaging observation:
• Flyby on 1 Nov 2023, closest approach 425 km at relative speed 4.5 km/s; Lucy carried only cameras (L'LORRI, T2CAM) and made no physical contact or intervention [Lucy SWRI encounter page].
• Imaging constrained morphology (trough Sumak Fossa, ridge Fab Dorsum, mass wasting) and discovered the first confirmed contact-binary satellite Selam [Levison et al. 2024 Nature].
• Formation hypotheses (YORP spin-up → mass shedding → debris disk → reaccretion; or multi-moonlet mergers) were inferred from geometry and dynamics, not measured by intervention [Raducan et al. 2025 Nature Communications; Bierhaus et al. 2025 PSJ].

(2) SEPARATE MUTUAL-ORBIT vs. HELIOCENTRIC QUANTITIES (DART ONLY)

Mutual orbit (Dimorphos around Didymos):
• Pre-impact period: 11.92148 ± 0.00013 h; post-impact: 11.372 ± 0.017 h [Thomas et al. 2023] → ΔP = −33.0 ± 1.0 min (3σ).
• Refined: −33 min 15 s (±1.5 s), final period 11h 22m 3s; semimajor axis decreased by 37 m; shape changed oblate spheroid → triaxial ellipsoid [Naidu et al. 2024].
• Along-track velocity change: Δv_T = −2.70 ± 0.10 mm/s [Cheng et al. 2023].
• Momentum enhancement β: 2.2–4.9 for bulk density 1,500–3,300 kg/m³; β = 3.61 (+0.19/−0.25) at nominal equal-density ρ = 2,400 kg/m³ [Cheng et al. 2023].

Heliocentric orbit (Didymos system barycenter around Sun):
• Along-track velocity change: −11.7 ± 1.3 μm/s (9σ detection) [Makadia et al. 2026].
• Corresponds to Δa = −360 ± 40 m and ΔP_orb = −150 ± 20 ms of the 2.11-yr solar orbit [Makadia et al. 2026].
• Measured via ~6000 astrometric points, 22 stellar occultations, 3 optical navigation points, 9 radar delay measurements [Makadia et al. 2026].

Note: The heliocentric change is ~6 orders of magnitude smaller than the mutual-orbit change because the momentum deposited in Dimorphos is shared between the binary's internal orbit (large effect) and the center-of-mass motion (tiny effect).

(3) GENERALIZATION LIMITS AND DEPENDENCIES

Dependent on object identity (cannot generalize to different target):
• Size: DART tested a ~160 m body; a much larger asteroid would require proportionally more kinetic energy and longer warning time [NASA Didymos page].
• Binary geometry: DART targeted a secondary moonlet in a close binary (separation ~3.4 km). A single asteroid would respond differently.
• Dimorphos specifically: formed through mass shedding from Didymos, giving it distinct properties [Raducan et al. 2024].

Dependent on structure:
• Rubble-pile: Dimorphos has macroporosity ~35%, surface cohesion < few Pa, boulder fraction <40 vol% [Raducan et al. 2024]. A monolithic or cohesive body would produce lower β and different deformation.
• β depends on Dimorphos mass/density (unknown, treated as variable 1,500–3,300 kg/m³) [Cheng et al. 2023]. Generalization to other density regimes requires new modeling.

Dependent on geometry and impact conditions:
• Head-on collision with leading hemisphere maximized momentum transfer [Thomas et al. 2023]. Different impact angle/velocity would change β.
• Ejecta contribution dominates total momentum (β > 1); ejecta cone opening angle ~139° constrains material properties [Raducan et al. 2024].

Dependent on measurement time:
• Mutual orbit: measurements span pre-impact (years of lightcurves) through post-impact weeks-to-months; period continued evolving after initial impact as ejecta escaped [Naidu et al. 2024].
• Heliocentric: required ~3+ years of astrometric follow-up after impact to detect μm/s-level change [Makadia et al. 2026].
• Lucy observations are snapshot constraints from a single 425-km flyby; long-term evolution (YORP spin-up timescale 10–20 Myr) is modeled, not measured directly [Bierhaus et al. 2025].

Dependent on model choice:
• β calculation uses Monte Carlo sampling of 12 unknown input parameters (shapes, density, ejecta direction) [Cheng et al. 2023].
• Heliocentric Δv derived from orbit determination filter estimating nongravitational Yarkovsky + impulse at impact epoch [Makadia et al. 2026].
• Lucy formation hypotheses depend on assumed YORP strength, internal friction angles, and collisional environment models [Raducan et al. 2025; Bierhaus et al. 2025].

Cannot be generalized:
• β = 2.2–4.9 and the 33-min period change are specific to Dimorphos's size, rubble-pile structure, and impact conditions. A different target (different size, density, cohesion, porosity) would yield different outcomes.
• Warning time requirement: 'several years at a minimum, but preferably decades' applies to planetary defense scenarios, not to the DART experiment itself [NASA Marshall page; Daly/Ernst/Barnouin et al. 2023 Nature].
• Lucy's morphological conclusions (contact binary Selam, trough/ridge formation) are specific to Dinkinesh's size (~720 m), S-type composition, and main-belt location; they cannot be projected to DART-like NEA binaries without separate justification.

(4) KEY PAPER CITATIONS

DART:
• Thomas et al. 2023 Nature 622, 491–496 — Mutual orbit period change −33.0 ± 1.0 min: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05805-2
• Cheng et al. 2023 Nature 622, 537–542 — Momentum transfer, β = 2.2–4.9: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05878-z
• Naidu et al. 2024 Planetary Science Journal — Refined period 33 min 15 s, shape change: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasa-study-asteroids-orbit-shape-changed-after-dart-impact/
• Makadia et al. 2026 Science Advances — Heliocentric Δv = −11.7 ± 1.3 μm/s: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aea4259
• Raducan et al. 2024 Communications Earth & Environment — Rubble-pile structure, porosity ~35%: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-024-02200-3
• NASA Marshall summary (four Nature papers): https://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/marshall/nasas-dart-data-validates-kinetic-impact-as-planetary-defense-method/
• NASA Didymos/Dimorphos overview: https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/asteroids/didymos/

Lucy:
• Levison et al. 2024 Nature 631, 322–327 — Contact binary satellite Selam discovery: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19337 (preprint); DOI 10.1038/s41586-024-07378-0
• Bierhaus et al. 2025 Planetary Science Journal — Geology of Dinkinesh/Selam, YORP-driven mass shedding: https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/PSJ/ae1968
• Raducan et al. 2025 Nature Communications 16, 11659 — Multiple moonlet mergers origin: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-66484-3
• NASA Lucy Dinkinesh flyby release: https://www.nasa.gov/solar-system/asteroids/nasa-lucy-images-reveal-asteroid-dinkinesh-to-be-surprisingly-complex/
• Lucy encounter basics: https://lucy.swri.edu/DinkineshEncounter.html

evidence.snippet: Thomas et al. 2023 report pre-impact period 11.92148 ± 0.00013 h, post-impact 11.372 ± 0.017 h, period change −33.0 ± 1.0 min (3σ). Two independent methods (lightcurve-only and radar+lightcurve+DRACO astrometry) agree. Expected simple-transfer change was ~7 min; observed change implies substantial ejecta momentum enhancement.
evidence.supports: Mutual orbit period change of Dimorphos by DART kinetic impact; baseline for β calculation.

evidence.snippet: Makadia et al. 2026 report first measurement of human-caused heliocentric deflection: Didymos system along-track Δv = −11.7 ± 1.3 μm/s (9σ), corresponding to −360 ± 40 m semimajor axis change and −150 ± 20 ms reduction in 2.1-yr solar orbit period. Derived from ~6000 astrometric, 22 occultation, 3 ON-point, 9 radar measurements.
evidence.supports: Heliocentric velocity change of the Didymos system after DART; separate from mutual-orbit quantity.

evidence.snippet: Cheng et al. 2023 derive instantaneous Δv_T = −2.70 ± 0.10 mm/s from the 33-min period change; momentum enhancement factor β ranges 2.2–4.9 for bulk density 1,500–3,300 kg/m³, with β = 3.61 (+0.19/−0.25) at nominal equal-density ρ = 2,400 kg/m³. Monte Carlo over 12 input parameters including density and shapes.
evidence.supports: Momentum enhancement β and its dependence on Dimorphos mass/density; demonstrates ejecta-dominated momentum transfer.

evidence.snippet: Naidu et al. 2024: immediate post-impact period shortened by 32 min 42 s to 11h 22m 37s; continued shortening as material escaped, settling at 33 min 15 s less (final 11h 22m 3s, ±1.5 s). Semimajor axis decreased by 37 m to 1,152 m. Shape changed from oblate spheroid to triaxial ellipsoid.
evidence.supports: Refined orbital period change and concurrent shape change; shows post-impact evolution continued beyond initial impulse.

evidence.snippet: Raducan et al. 2024: Dimorphos bulk density <2,400 kg/m³, macroporosity 38 ± 3% (local SFD) and 34 ± 4% (global SFD); rubble-pile structure; surface cohesion < few Pa (≤500 Pa upper bound); boulder fraction <40 vol% for >2.5 m boulders. Impact caused global deformation, no conventional crater. Supports formation via mass shedding from Didymos.
evidence.supports: Dimorphos rubble-pile structure and physical properties that determine β and impact response; not generic to all asteroids.

evidence.snippet: Levison et al. 2024: Lucy flyby within 431 km of Dinkinesh (effective diameter ~720 m) revealed longitudinal trough, equatorial ridge, and first confirmed contact binary satellite Selam (lobes ~210 m and ~230 m, orbital distance 3.1 km, period ~52.7 hr, tidally locked). Ridge/trough inferred from YORP spin-up mass failure and partial reaccretion; Selam accreted from shed material.
evidence.supports: Lucy provided imaging constraints on morphology and formation hypothesis only—no intervention occurred; Selam's contact-binary nature is a structural observation.

evidence.snippet: Bierhaus et al. 2025: Dinkinesh geology includes Sumak Fossa (trough), Fab Dorsum (ridge, volume 1.51×10^7 m³), mass wasting; crater SFD slope c = 1.09 ± 0.05 suggests young surface; YORP spin-up timescale 10–20 Myr; Dinkinesh has rubble-pile structure with weak surface (~Pa) and slightly stronger interior. Selam could have formed via YORP-driven mass shedding or other mechanisms.
evidence.supports: Lucy-derived geological constraints and formation hypotheses for Dinkinesh/Selam; dependent on Dinkinesh's size and main-belt location.

evidence.snippet: Raducan et al. 2025: Selam likely formed through low-velocity mergers of similarly-sized moonlets (v/v_esc 0.75–2); Selam A ridge requires surface cohesion <~1 Pa and boulder fraction <22 vol%; Selam B merger at v/v_esc 1–1.25. Dinkinesh-like systems may represent an unknown sub-population; forming wide contact-binary satellite requires multiple spin-up/shedding events—poses challenges for efficient formation.
evidence.supports: Formation hypotheses for Selam are model-dependent inferences from Lucy morphology; not measured by intervention.

evidence.snippet: NASA confirms DART impact altered Dimorphos orbit by 33 min; beta amplified 2.2–4.9 depending on Dimorphos mass. Intercepting ~half-mile asteroid achievable without advance reconnaissance but requires sufficient warning time—several years minimum, preferably decades. DART turned Dimorphos into an active asteroid (first observation of impact-induced activation).
evidence.supports: Warning time requirements and operational implications for planetary defense; generalization limits for future missions.

evidence.snippet: Didymos ~780 m diameter; Dimorphos ~160 m diameter. DART impacted Dimorphos at ~6.6 km/s on 26 Sept 2022. Pre-impact mutual period 11h 55m shortened to 11h 23m (±2 min early announcement). Success threshold was 73 seconds; DART surpassed by >25×. Didymos orbits Sun in 2.11 yr, classified Amor NEA.
evidence.supports: Basic sizes, dates, and success criteria for DART; Dimorphos size (~160 m) is a generalization limit.

evidence.snippet: Lucy Dinkinesh encounter: 1 Nov 2023, closest approach 425 km, encounter speed 4.5 km/s. Primary est. 790 m, secondary 220 m. Instruments: L'LORRI and T2CAM cameras only. No physical contact or intervention performed.
evidence.supports: Lucy flyby was purely observational; imaging instruments only, confirming non-intervention nature of the mission.
